newsitem.title: UK: LME base metals end sharply lower on fund-led slum.
newsitem.headline: LME base metals end sharply lower on fund-led slum.

text.p: The base metals staged a minor recovery on the London Metal Exchange on Monday afternoon after racking up heavy losses from aggressive fund selling earlier in the day.
But the afternoon kerb closes remained well below those posted last Friday.
"It's been a rollercoaster day, although more down than up," said analyst Robin Bhar of brokers Brandeis.
The fund selling which swept all the metals sharply lower in the morning and midday trading session tapered off in the afternoon, helping to stabilise prices, he said.
Traders reported some trade selling emerging at the lows, but not in substantial volumes, as the market waited for prices to decline still further.
Flagship three-months copper ended the session at $2,278 per tonne, a decline of $58, having bounced from a low of $2,264.
But prices were still vulnerable to $2,250, or even $2,200, before resuming an upwards course, some analysts said.
Cash to threes backwardation was narrower at $33/$35, compared to $40/$45 at the start of the day.
Aluminium was similarly off lows but still substantially weaker at $1,583, a decline of $41, after it sank below the $1,600 early in the day.
Some traders said the fund sell-off in all the base metals was probably sparked by losses sustained by aluminium futures on the Tokyo TOCOM exchange amid speculative selling.

But some of the selling appeared to be distress sales by funds who had been caught out in other markets, Bhar noted. Gyrations in stock and bond markets may yet have further repercussions in the metals, he added.
The start of daily LME stock reporting was said by most traders to have had little effect on prices, but the market would be watching the figures closely in coming weeks.
Zinc, which showed a stocks rise of 5,000 tonnes, was sold down sharply by the funds and ran into stop loss selling.
It ended $20 lower at $1,247.
The market had been expecting a stock increase for weeks and probably took it in stride. But the hike may have encouraged funds already intending to take profits on zinc, analysts and dealers said.
Tin, which had plummeted by $200 to a near two-year low during the midday trading session, pared half of its losses, ending $100 weaker at $5,720.
Nickel, however, ended near its lows and finished $180 weaker at $7,290.
Lead prices finished $19 lower at $650, having bounced from a low of $636.
Cash-threes moved into a $2/$2.5 contango after being in a $9/$11 backwardation at the start of last week.
Alloy was $30 down at $1,485.
--Lida Poletz, London newsroom +44 171 542 2936
